moduleTitle: Jesus Christ and salvation: the incarnation and Jesus as the Son of God

note.specFocus: Spec: Jesus Christ and salvation — beliefs and teachings about the incarnation and Jesus as the Son of God.
note.summary:
The incarnation
• Incarnation means 'becoming flesh': God the Son took on a human nature and was born as Jesus of Nazareth.
• 'The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us' (John 1:14). The Word, who 'was God' (John 1:1), became a real human being.
• Jesus is fully God and fully human — two natures in one person (Council of Chalcedon, 451). He was not half-and-half, nor God pretending to be human.

The birth narratives (Matthew 1–2 and Luke 1–2)
• Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary (the virgin birth / virginal conception).
• The Annunciation: the angel Gabriel tells Mary, 'The Holy Spirit will come on you… the holy one to be born will be called the Son of God' (Luke 1:35).
• Joseph is told the child will be called 'Immanuel — which means "God with us"' (Matthew 1:23).
• Born in Bethlehem in humble circumstances, laid in a manger (Luke 2:7); visited by shepherds (Luke) and Magi (Matthew).

Evidence of Jesus' humanity and divinity in the Gospels
• Human: born, grew up, felt hunger, tiredness, temptation (Matthew 4), wept (John 11:35), suffered and died.
• Divine: miracles; forgiving sins (Mark 2:5–7); transfiguration; resurrection; claims such as 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30).

Jesus as the Son of God
• At his baptism: 'You are my Son, whom I love; with you I am well pleased' (Mark 1:11).
• 'Son of God' expresses a unique relationship with the Father and a shared divine nature — not a biological relationship.
• The Nicene Creed: 'the only Son of God, eternally begotten of the Father… true God from true God, begotten, not made, of one Being with the Father'.
• Other titles: Christ/Messiah ('anointed one'), Lord, Son of Man, Word (Logos), Immanuel.

Diversity of views
• Mainstream Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches all affirm the creeds.
• Some liberal Christians interpret the virgin birth symbolically, while still believing God was uniquely present in Jesus; traditional Christians insist it is historical.
• Catholics and Orthodox give Mary special honour as 'Mother of God' (Theotokos, Council of Ephesus 431) because of the incarnation; many Protestants honour her but place less emphasis on her.
• Non-Christian views: Muslims see Jesus as a prophet; humanists as a moral teacher.

Importance and influence
• Shows God's love: God entered the world to save it (John 3:16).
• Reveals God: 'Anyone who has seen me has seen the Father' (John 14:9).
• God understands human weakness (Hebrews 4:15), encouraging prayer.
• Jesus is a perfect example to follow; human life and the physical world are valuable.
• Celebrated at Christmas; affirmed in creeds and hymns.

Key terms: incarnation, virgin birth, Annunciation, Immanuel, Son of God, Messiah, Logos, Chalcedon, Theotokos.

questions.question:
Which one of the following best describes the incarnation?
A  Jesus rising from the dead
B  God becoming human in Jesus
C  Jesus returning to heaven
D  The Holy Spirit coming at Pentecost
questions.modelAnswer:
B — God becoming human in Jesus

The incarnation (from Latin 'in carne', 'in flesh') is the belief that God the Son took on human nature and became a human being in Jesus, while remaining fully God: 'The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us' (John 1:14). A is the resurrection, C is the ascension and D is Pentecost.
questions.examTip: Learn crisp one-line definitions for incarnation, resurrection, ascension and atonement.

questions.question:
Which one of the following Gospels records the angel telling Mary 'the holy one to be born will be called the Son of God'?
A  Mark
B  Luke
C  John
D  Acts
questions.modelAnswer:
B — Luke

Luke 1:35 records the angel Gabriel's words to Mary at the Annunciation: 'The Holy Spirit will come on you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. So the holy one to be born will be called the Son of God.' Mark and John do not include birth narratives, and Acts is not a Gospel.
questions.examTip: Only Matthew and Luke contain the birth stories of Jesus.

questions.question: Give one title used for Jesus that shows Christians believe he is divine.
questions.modelAnswer: Any one of, e.g.: Son of God; the Word (Logos); Lord; Emmanuel ('God with us', Matthew 1:23); the Christ/Messiah (accept, as Christians understand this title); God the Son.

questions.question: Give one reason why Christians believe Jesus was fully human.
questions.modelAnswer:
Any one of, e.g.:
• He was born of a human mother, Mary.
• He experienced hunger, tiredness and thirst.
• He wept at the death of Lazarus (John 11:35).
• He felt pain and died on the cross.
• He was tempted (Matthew 4:1–11).

questions.question: Explain two ways in which belief in the incarnation influences Christians today.
questions.modelAnswer:
First way: Because Christians believe God became human in Jesus, they see Jesus' life as the perfect example of how to live. They try to copy his compassion, forgiveness and humility, for example by caring for the sick and marginalised as he did, asking 'What would Jesus do?'

Second way: Belief that God 'became flesh' (John 1:14) shows that God values human life and the physical world. This influences Christians to treat every person with dignity, to celebrate Christmas as a major festival of God's love, and to feel that God understands their struggles because he lived a human life — giving them confidence to pray.
questions.examTip: Each way should describe a real-life effect on belief or behaviour.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which belief that Jesus is the Son of God influences Christians today.
questions.modelAnswer:
First way: Because Jesus is the Son of God, Christians worship him and pray to him or through him, ending many prayers 'through Jesus Christ our Lord'. His words carry divine authority, so Christians treat the Gospels as central to worship — standing for the Gospel reading in many churches.

Second way: Christians believe that through Jesus, the Son, they can become children of God themselves (John 1:12). This gives them a sense of identity and belonging in God's family, encouraging them to treat other Christians as brothers and sisters and to share their faith with others through evangelism.
questions.examTip: Use specific worship practices to develop points.

questions.question:
Explain two Christian teachings about the incarnation.

Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First teaching: Jesus is fully God and fully human. John's Gospel teaches 'The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us' (John 1:14) — the eternal Word, who 'was God' (John 1:1), took on a real human body and nature. The Council of Chalcedon (451) taught that Jesus has two natures, divine and human, united in one person, without mixing or confusion.

Second teaching: Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary. Matthew's Gospel says Mary 'was found to be pregnant through the Holy Spirit' (Matthew 1:18), and calls him 'Immanuel — which means "God with us"' (Matthew 1:23). This shows the incarnation was a miraculous act of God, not an ordinary birth.

Application: These teachings mean Christians believe God truly entered human life to save humanity; because Jesus shared human experience, 'we do not have a high priest who is unable to empathise with our weaknesses' (Hebrews 4:15).
questions.examTip: Name the gospel and verse, then say what it shows — this secures both source marks.

questions.question:
Explain two Christian teachings about Jesus as the Son of God.

Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First teaching: Jesus has a unique relationship with God the Father. At his baptism a voice from heaven said, 'You are my Son, whom I love; with you I am well pleased' (Mark 1:11). Christians believe this shows Jesus is the divine Son, not merely a good man or prophet.

Second teaching: As Son of God, Jesus is equal with the Father and shares his divine nature. Jesus said 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30), and the Nicene Creed calls him 'the only Son of God, eternally begotten of the Father… true God from true God… of one Being with the Father'. Christians believe this means Jesus can reveal God perfectly and has the authority to forgive sins.

Application: Jesus' miracles and resurrection are seen as signs of this identity; John wrote his Gospel 'that you may believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God' (John 20:31).
questions.examTip: 'Son of God' does not mean God had a child biologically — show you understand the theological meaning.

questions.question:
‘Jesus was just a good teacher, not the Son of God.’

Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Christian teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT OF THE STATEMENT

Many non-religious people and some other faiths accept that Jesus was a real historical figure who taught powerful moral lessons — love your enemies, forgive, care for the poor — but deny he was divine. Humanists, for example, admire his ethics without accepting supernatural claims. Muslims revere Jesus (Isa) as a great prophet, but reject the idea that God has a son.

Some scholars argue that the title 'Son of God' was used in Jewish tradition for kings and righteous people, and that belief in Jesus' full divinity developed later in the early Church, being formally defined at Nicaea in 325. Miracle stories and the virgin birth cannot be proved scientifically, so a sceptic might conclude Jesus was an inspiring human being whose followers later exalted him.

ARGUMENTS FOR A DIFFERENT VIEW

Christians believe the Gospels clearly present Jesus as more than a teacher. At his baptism the Father declares 'You are my Son' (Mark 1:11); Jesus forgives sins, which only God can do (Mark 2:5–7); and he claims 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30). John's Gospel opens by identifying Jesus as the eternal Word who 'was God' (John 1:1, 14).

C.S. Lewis argued that Jesus cannot simply have been a good teacher: someone who claimed to be God would either be lying, deluded, or telling the truth ('liar, lunatic or Lord'). A merely human teacher who made such claims would not be 'good'.

Above all, Christians point to the resurrection. Paul lists many witnesses who saw the risen Jesus (1 Corinthians 15:3–8), and the disciples, once frightened, were willing to die for their belief. Christians argue this transformation is best explained if Jesus really is the Son of God. Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Christians all affirm in the Nicene Creed that he is 'true God from true God'.

JUSTIFIED CONCLUSION

From a non-religious perspective the statement is understandable, since the divinity of Jesus cannot be proved. However, the statement says Jesus was 'just' a good teacher, and this fits poorly with the evidence of the Gospels, where his teaching is bound up with claims about his own identity. If those claims were false, his goodness would be questionable. From a Christian standpoint, and considering Lewis's argument, I conclude that it is more coherent to see Jesus either as far more than a teacher or as something other than 'good' — and Christians, on the basis of scripture and the resurrection, believe he is the Son of God.
questions.examTip: Include a non-religious or other-faith view for the 'different point of view' — it is credited.

questions.question:
‘The incarnation is the most important event in Christianity.’

Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Christian teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT OF THE STATEMENT

Without the incarnation, nothing else in the Christian story could happen. Jesus could not die on the cross or rise from the dead unless God had first become human. John 1:14 — 'The Word became flesh' — is the starting point of salvation. Athanasius argued that God became human so that humans could share in God's life; for him the incarnation itself begins to heal humanity.

The incarnation shows the depth of God's love: God did not stay distant but entered the world as a vulnerable baby. It reveals what God is like ('Anyone who has seen me has seen the Father', John 14:9) and means God understands human suffering from the inside (Hebrews 4:15). Christmas is the most widely celebrated Christian festival in Britain, showing its importance to many people.

ARGUMENTS FOR A DIFFERENT VIEW

Most Christians would say that the crucifixion and resurrection are more important. Paul says 'if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile' (1 Corinthians 15:17), and that he preached 'Christ crucified' (1 Corinthians 1:23). The cross is the main symbol of Christianity, not the manger. Easter, not Christmas, is the oldest and holiest Christian festival.

Christians believe salvation comes through Jesus' death as an atonement for sin (Mark 10:45) and that the resurrection proves victory over death. The incarnation is the means to this end: Jesus was born in order to die and rise again.

Some Christians, such as Pentecostals, would also stress Pentecost as vital, since it is when the Spirit came and the Church was born (Acts 2).

JUSTIFIED CONCLUSION

The incarnation is essential — without it there would be no Jesus and no salvation — and it profoundly shows God's love. However, the statement claims it is the 'most important event'. Scripture and Christian worship place the death and resurrection at the centre: Easter is the greatest festival and the cross is the universal symbol. I conclude that the incarnation, crucifixion and resurrection form one connected story of salvation, but if one event must be chosen, the resurrection is more important because it confirms Jesus' identity and the hope of eternal life.
questions.examTip: Consider how events link together — evaluating relationships between beliefs is a higher-level skill.
